etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English hepe, from Old English hēap, from Proto-West Germanic *haup, from Proto-Germanic *haupaz (compare Dutch hoop, German Low German Hupen, German Haufen), from Proto-Indo-European *koupos (“hill”) (compare Lithuanian kaũpas, Albanian qipi (“stack”), Avestan 𐬐𐬂𐬟𐬀 (kåfa)).

definitions.definition: A crowd; a throng; a multitude or great number of people.

quote.citation: 1622 (date written), Francis [Bacon], “An Advertisement Touching an Holy VVarre. […]”, in William Rawley, editor, Certaine Miscellany VVorks of the Right Honourable Francis Lo. Verulam, Viscount S. Alban. […], London:  […]  I. Hauiland for Humphrey Robinson, […], published 1629, →OCLC, page 104:
quote.text: A Heap of Vassals, and Slaues:  […]  A People that is without Naturall Affection,  […]  A Nation without Morality, without Letters, Arts, or Sciences

quote.citation: 1858, Anthony Trollope, Doctor Thorne. […], volume (please specify |volume=I to III), London: Chapman & Hall, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: He had plenty of friends, heaps of friends in the parliamentary sense

definitions.definition: A pile or mass; a collection of things laid in a body, or thrown together so as to form an elevation.

quote.citation: 1697, Virgil, “(please specify the book number)”, in John Dryden, transl., The Works of Virgil: Containing His Pastorals, Georgics, and Æneis. […], London:  […]  Jacob Tonson, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: Huge heaps of slain around the body rise.

quote.citation: 2012 May 9, Jonathan Wilson, “Europa League: Radamel Falcao's Atlético Madrid rout Athletic Bilbao”, in the Guardian‎[1]:
quote.text: Every break seemed dangerous and Falcao clearly had the beating of Amorebieta. Others, being forced to stretch a foot behind them to control Arda Turan's 34th-minute cross, might simply have lashed a shot on the turn; Falcao, though, twisted back on to his left foot, leaving Amorebieta in a heap, and thumped in an inevitable finish – his 12th goal in 15 European matches this season.

definitions.definition: A great number or large quantity of things.

quote.citation: 1679, Gilbert Burnet, The History of the Reformation of the Church of England:
quote.text: a vast heap, both of places of scripture and quotations

quote.citation: 1878, Robert Louis Stevenson, Will o' the Mill:
quote.text: I have noticed a heap of things in my life.

definitions.definition: (computing) A data structure consisting of trees in which each node is greater than all its children.

quote.citation: 1991 May 12, “Kidnapped!”, in Jeeves and Wooster, Series 2, Episode 5:
quote.text: Chuffy: It's on a knife edge at the moment, Bertie. If he can get planning permission, old Stoker's going to take this heap off my hands in return for vast amounts of oof.

quote.citation: 1848 November – 1850 December, William Makepeace Thackeray, chapter 10, in The History of Pendennis. […], volume (please specify |volume=I or II), London: Bradbury and Evans, […], published 1849–1850, →OCLC:
quote.text: [W]e went to the play, and Pen was struck all of a heap with Miss Fotheringay … And he’s fallen in love with her—and I’m blessed if he hasn’t proposed to her  […]

definitions.definition: (transitive) To form or round into a heap, as in measuring.

quote.citation: 1819, John Keats, Otho the Great, act I, scene II, verses 40-42:
quote.text: Cry a reward, to him who shall first bring  News of that vanished Arabian,  A full-heap’d helmet of the purest gold.

quote.citation: 2022 January 12, Nigel Harris, “Comment: Unhappy start to 2022”, in RAIL, number 948, page 3:
quote.text: Then, in January, a creeping tsunami of train cancellations, triggered by major staff absences as a result of the aggressive transmissibility of Omicron, heaped further misery on rail users.

definitions.definition: (possibly offensive) very; representing broken English stereotypically or comically attributed to Native Americans

quote.citation: 1980, Joey Lee Dillard, Perspectives on American English, page 417:
quote.text: We are all familiar with the stereotyped broken English which writers of Western stories, comic strips, and similar literature put into the mouths of Indians: 'me heap big chief', 'you like um fire water', and so forth.

quote.citation: 2004, John Robert Colombo, The Penguin Book of Canadian Jokes, page 175:
quote.text: Once upon a time, a Scotsman, an Englishman, and an Irishman are captured by the Red Indians  […]  He approaches the Englishman, pinches the skin of his upper arm, and says, "Hmmm, heap good skin, nice and thick.
